title: Asking AI About Your Health or How You Feel
description: When an AI chatbot can genuinely help with a health or wellbeing question, the honest risks of leaning on it about your body or your mind, and the one rule that keeps you safe, plus exactly where to turn for real help in Canada. Free lesson, no account needed.
lesson_time: About 15 minutes, at your own pace
lead: When an AI chatbot can genuinely help with a health or wellbeing question, the real risks of leaning on it about your body or your mind, and the one rule that keeps you safe, plus exactly where to turn for real help in Canada. If you are struggling right now, you can skip straight to "Where to find real help in Canada" below, any time.

story.label: Why this lesson exists
paragraphs: More and more people are typing health questions, and private worries about how they feel, into AI chatbots. It is easy to understand why. The chatbot is there at three in the morning. It never makes you wait, never sends a bill, and never seems to judge you.
This lesson is not here to scold you for that. It is here to help you use these tools wisely about the two things that matter most: your body and your mind.

coach: If you have turned to a chatbot because it felt easier than telling a real person, I want you to know that makes complete sense. Reaching for something private and always available is a very human thing to do. None of what follows is a telling-off. I just want you to have the full picture, so the tool stays a helper and never becomes a substitute for the care you deserve.

sections.text: Why people turn to AI for this
Let us be fair to the tool first, because the reasons are real.

items: It is available any time, day or night, with no appointment and no waiting list.
It is free, and it never makes you feel rushed or embarrassed.
It can help you put a worry into words, which is sometimes the hardest part.
It can help you prepare questions before you see a real doctor or nurse.
For someone who feels too anxious or ashamed to talk to a person, it can feel like a gentle first step.

sections.text: Those are genuine benefits. A first step can matter. The trouble starts when the first step becomes the only step.
The honest risks (this is the important part)
Here is the part the chatbot will not tell you about itself.
It is built to agree with you

AI chatbots are designed to be pleasant and affirming. They tend to tell you what you want to hear. That is the opposite of what good health and mental-health advice often has to do, which is to gently tell you something you might not want to hear, like "please go and see someone about this."
It can be confidently wrong

A chatbot can state a wrong fact about a medication, a symptom, or a dose in the same calm, certain voice it uses for correct ones. It does not know your history, your other medications, or your body. And it is not a crisis service; no one is accountable for its advice.
Feeling helped is not the same as being helped

This is the heart of it. Because the chatbot is so agreeable, talking to it often feels supportive. That good feeling is exactly the trap. It can quietly take the place of talking to a real person, and that can leave you more alone with the problem, not less.

sections.label: What the research is starting to show
sections.text: In a 2026 United States survey by KFF, about one in three adults said they had used an AI chatbot for health information: 29 percent for physical health and 16 percent for mental health. These are US figures; comparable Canadian numbers are not yet widely published, so treat them as a signal of a growing habit, not an exact Canadian count.
The one rule

sections.label: Remember this one line
sections.text: AI can be a starting point, never the final word, on your body or your mind. For anything real, take it to a doctor or a person you trust.
That is the whole lesson in a sentence. Use the chatbot to gather your thoughts or draft your questions if it helps. Then bring those questions to a real person who can be responsible for the answer.
Where to find real help in Canada
If the question is about how you are feeling, please do not leave it with a chatbot. These are real Canadian services, staffed by real people, and they are free.
If you are in distress or thinking about harming yourself

Call or text 988, the Suicide Crisis Helpline. It is free, available any time, in English or French, anywhere in Canada. You can also call Talk Suicide Canada at 1-833-456-4566. You do not need to be in crisis to call. If you are not sure, that is a good enough reason to reach out.
For a health question or worry

In Ontario, dial 811 for Health811 to speak with a registered nurse, free, any time. Your family doctor or pharmacist can answer most everyday health and medication questions. A pharmacist is free to talk to and needs no appointment.
To find local support of any kind
Dial 211 to reach a real person who can connect you to local mental-health, community, and seniors' services near you. It is free, confidential, and available in many languages.

sections.label: The move is
sections.text: Use a chatbot to put a worry into words or draft questions if that helps you start. Then take anything real about your body or your mind to a real person: your doctor, your pharmacist, Health811 (dial 811), or 988 if you are in distress.

sections.heading: Quick check: test your knowledge
sections.intro: Tap the answer you think is correct. There is no score kept and nothing to sign in to.

questions.q: 1. What is a genuinely good use of an AI chatbot for health?
options: Getting a diagnosis for a new symptom
Deciding whether to stop a medication
Putting a worry into words and preparing questions for your doctor
Replacing counselling when you feel low
questions.right: Right. It can help you find the words and prepare questions. The answers themselves still belong with a real person who knows you and is accountable.
questions.wrong: The safe use is preparation: putting a worry into words and drafting questions to bring to a real doctor, nurse, or pharmacist. Diagnosis, medication changes, and emotional support belong with real people.

questions.q: 2. Why is it a problem that chatbots are built to be agreeable?
options: It makes them slower to answer
They may tell you what you want to hear instead of what you need to hear
It makes them more expensive
It is not a problem
questions.right: Exactly. Good health advice sometimes has to say "please go and see someone about this." An agreeable chatbot tends not to, and that comfortable feeling is the trap.
questions.wrong: Agreeable chatbots tend to tell you what you want to hear. Good health and mental-health advice sometimes needs to gently tell you what you do not want to hear, like "please see someone about this."

questions.q: 3. "Feeling helped is not the same as being helped" means:
options: Chatbots never help anyone
A supportive-feeling chat can quietly replace the real help that would actually make a difference
You should never talk about feelings
Real help always feels unpleasant
questions.right: Right. Because the chatbot feels supportive, it can take the place of talking to a real person, leaving you more alone with the problem, not less.
questions.wrong: It means the comforting feeling of a chatbot conversation can quietly stand in for real care, so the problem stays unaddressed. The feeling of support is not the same as actual help.

questions.q: 4. What is the one rule from this lesson?
options: Never use AI for anything health-related
Trust AI for small things, doctors for big things
AI is a starting point, never the final word, on your body or your mind
Always ask two different chatbots
questions.right: That is the whole lesson in a sentence. Use it to gather your thoughts, then take anything real to a person who can be responsible for the answer.
questions.wrong: The rule is: AI can be a starting point, never the final word, on your body or your mind. For anything real, take it to a doctor or a person you trust.

questions.q: 5. You are in distress and need to talk to someone right now, anywhere in Canada. What do you do?
options: Ask a chatbot for coping strategies
Call or text 988, free, any time
Wait until your next appointment
Search online for advice
questions.right: Right. 988 is the Suicide Crisis Helpline: call or text, free, any time, in English or French. You do not need to be in crisis to reach out.
questions.wrong: Call or text 988, the Suicide Crisis Helpline: free, any time, anywhere in Canada, in English or French. A real person will answer. You do not need to be certain it is a crisis to call.

sections.heading: Your progress
sections.intro: Tick each item as you feel confident with it. This is saved on this device only, with no account needed.
items: I know why a chatbot can feel like a safe place to bring health worries, and why that feeling can be a trap
I know a chatbot can be confidently wrong and does not know my history or medications
I can say the one rule: AI is a starting point, never the final word, on my body or my mind
I know the real Canadian helps: 988, Health811 (dial 811 in Ontario), 211, my doctor, and my pharmacist
I know I can bring chatbot-drafted questions to a real appointment

success_state: Well done. You now know the honest picture: a chatbot can be a private first step, but it agrees with you to a fault, it can be confidently wrong, and feeling helped is not the same as being helped. The rule is simple: a starting point, never the final word, on your body or your mind. And if you ever need a real person, 988, Health811, and 211 are there for you, free, any time.
